{{technical|date=October 2022}}

In [[mathematics]], '''Rathjen's <math>\psi</math> psi function''' is an [[ordinal collapsing function]] developed by Michael Rathjen. It collapses [[Mahlo cardinal|weakly Mahlo cardinals]] <math>M</math> to generate [[large countable ordinal]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rathjen|first=Michael|date=1990|title=Ordinal Notation Based on a Weakly Mahlo Cardinal|url=http://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Ord_Notation_Weakly_Mahlo.pdf|access-date=2021-09-18|website=University of Leeds|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231208185422/http://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/Ord_Notation_Weakly_Mahlo.pdf|archive-date=2023-12-08}}</ref> A weakly Mahlo cardinal is a cardinal such that the set of [[regular cardinal]]s below <math>M</math> is closed under <math>M</math> (i.e. all [[normal function]]s closed in <math>M</math> are closed under some regular ordinal <math>< M</math>). Rathjen uses this to diagonalise over the [[Inaccessible cardinal|weakly inaccessible]] hierarchy.

It admits an associated ordinal notation <math>T(M)</math> whose limit (i.e. ordinal type) is <math>\psi_\Omega(\chi_{\varepsilon_M+1}(0))</math>, which is strictly greater than both <math>\vert KPM\vert</math> and the limit of countable ordinals expressed by Rathjen's <math>\psi</math>. <math>\vert KPM\vert</math>, which is called the "Small Rathjen ordinal" is the proof-theoretic ordinal of <math>\mathsf{KPM}</math>, [[Kripke–Platek set theory]] augmented by the [[axiom schema]] "for any <math>\Delta_0</math>-formula <math>H(x, y)</math> satisfying <math>\forall x \, \exists y\,(H(x, y))</math>, there exists an addmissible set <math>z</math> satisfying <math>\forall x \in z \, \exists y\,(H(x, y))</math>". It is equal to <math>\psi_\Omega(\psi_{\chi_{\varepsilon_M+1}(0)}(0))</math> in Rathjen's <math>\psi</math> function.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Rathjen|first=Michael|date=1994-01-01|title=Collapsing functions based on recursively large ordinals: A well-ordering proof for KPM|url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01275469|journal=Archive for Mathematical Logic|language=en|volume=33|issue=1|pages=35–55|doi=10.1007/BF01275469|s2cid=35012853|issn=1432-0665|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Restrict <math>\pi</math> and <math>\kappa</math> to uncountable regular cardinals <math>< M</math>; for a function <math>f</math> let <math>\operatorname{dom}(f)</math> denote the domain of <math>f</math>; let <math>\operatorname{cl}_M(X)</math> denote <math>X \cup \{\alpha < M: \alpha \text{ is a limit point of } X\}</math>, and let <math>\operatorname{enum}(X)</math> denote the [[enumeration]] of <math>X</math>. Lastly, an ordinal <math>\alpha</math> is said to be to be '''strongly critical''' if <math>\varphi_\alpha(0) = \alpha</math>.

For <math>\alpha \in \Gamma_{M+1}</math> and <math>\beta \in M</math>:

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \beta \cup \{0, M\} \subseteq B^n(\alpha, \beta) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \gamma_1 + \cdots + \gamma_k \land \gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_k \in B^n(\alpha,\beta) \rightarrow \gamma \in B^{n+1}(\alpha, \beta) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \varphi_{\gamma_0}(\gamma_1) \land \gamma_0, \gamma_1 \in B^n(\alpha,\beta) \rightarrow \gamma \in B^{n+1}(\alpha, \beta) \\[5pt]
& \pi \in B^n(\alpha,\beta) \land \gamma < \pi \rightarrow \gamma \in B^{n+1}(\alpha, \beta) \\[5pt]
& \delta, \eta \in B^n(\alpha,\beta) \land \delta < \alpha \land \eta \in \operatorname{dom}(\chi_\delta) \rightarrow \chi_\delta(\eta) \in B^{n+1}(\alpha,\beta)  \\[5pt]
& B(\alpha,\beta) = \bigcup_{n < \omega}B^n(\alpha, \beta) \\[5pt]
& \chi_\alpha = \operatorname{enum}(\operatorname{cl_M}(\{\kappa: \kappa \notin B(\alpha, \kappa) \land \alpha \in B(\alpha,\kappa)\}))
\end{align}
</math>

If <math>\kappa = \chi_\alpha(\beta+1)</math> for some <math>(\alpha,\beta) \in \Gamma_{M+1} \times M</math>, define <math>\kappa^- := \chi_\alpha(\beta)</math> using the unique <math>(\alpha,\beta)</math>. Otherwise if <math>\kappa = \chi_\alpha(0)</math> for some <math>\alpha \in \Gamma_{M+1}</math>, then define <math>\kappa^- := \sup(\operatorname{SC}_M(\alpha) \cup \{0\})</math> using the unique <math>\alpha</math>, where <math>\operatorname{SC}_M(\alpha)</math> is a set of strongly critical ordinals <math>< M</math> explicitly defined in the original source.

For <math>\alpha \in \Gamma_{M+1}</math>:

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \kappa^- \cup \{\kappa^-, M\} \subset C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \gamma_1 + \cdots+ \gamma_k \text{ and } \gamma_1, \ldots, \gamma_k \in C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \rightarrow \gamma \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \varphi_{\gamma_0}(\gamma_1) \land \gamma_0, \gamma_1 \in C_\kappa^n(\alpha,\beta) \rightarrow \gamma \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \pi \in C^n_\kappa(\alpha) \cap \kappa \land \gamma < \pi \land \pi \in \textrm{R} \rightarrow \gamma \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \chi_\delta(\eta) \land \delta, \eta \in C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \rightarrow \gamma \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \gamma = \Phi_\delta(\eta) \land \delta, \eta \in C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \land 0 < \delta \land \delta, \eta < M \rightarrow \gamma \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \beta < \alpha \land \pi, \beta \in C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \land \beta \in C_\pi(\beta) \rightarrow \psi_\pi(\beta) \in C_\kappa^{n+1}(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& C_\kappa(\alpha) := \bigcup_{n < \omega}C_\kappa^n(\alpha) \\[5pt]
& \psi_\kappa(\alpha) := \min(\{\xi:\xi\notin C_\kappa(\alpha)\})
\end{align}
</math>

== Explanation ==

* Restrict <math>\pi</math> to uncountable regular cardinals.
* <math>\operatorname{enum}(X)</math> is a unique increasing function such that the range of <math>\operatorname{enum}(X)</math> is exactly <math>X</math>.
* <math>\operatorname{cl}(X)</math> is the closure of <math>X</math>, i.e. <math>X \cup \{\beta \in \operatorname{Lim} \mid \sup(X \cap \beta) = \beta\}</math>, where <math>\operatorname{Lim}</math> denotes the [[Class (set theory)|class]] of non-zero [[limit ordinal]]s.
* <math>B_0(\alpha, \beta) = \beta \cup \{0, M\}</math>
* <math>B_{n+1}(\alpha, \beta) = \{\gamma + \delta, \varphi_\gamma(\delta), \chi_\mu(\delta) | \gamma, \delta, \mu \in B_n(\alpha, \beta) \land \mu < \alpha\}</math>
* <math>B(\alpha, \beta) = \bigcup_{n < \omega}B_n(\alpha, \beta)</math>
* <math>\chi_\alpha(\beta) = \operatorname{enum}(\operatorname{cl}(\{\pi: B(\alpha, \pi) \cap M \subseteq \pi \land \alpha \in B(\alpha, \pi)\})) = \operatorname{enum}(\{\beta \in \operatorname{Lim} \mid \sup \{\pi: B(\alpha, \pi) \cap M \subseteq \pi \land \alpha \in B(\alpha, \pi)\} \cap \beta) = \beta\}</math>
* <math>C_0(\alpha, \beta) = \beta \cup \{0, M\}</math>
* <math>C_{n+1}(\alpha, \beta) = \{\gamma + \delta, \varphi_\gamma(\delta), \chi_\mu(\delta), \psi_\pi(\mu) | \gamma, \delta, \mu, \pi \in B_n(\alpha, \beta) \land \mu < \alpha\}</math>
* <math>C(\alpha, \beta) = \bigcup_{n < \omega}C_n(\alpha, \beta)</math>
* <math>\psi_\pi(\alpha) = \min(\{\beta: C(\alpha, \beta) \cap \pi \subseteq \beta \land \alpha \in C(\alpha, \beta)\})</math>

Rathjen originally defined the <math>\psi</math> function in more complicated a way in order to create an ordinal notation associated to it. Therefore, it is not certain whether the simplified OCF above yields an ordinal notation or not. The original <math>\chi</math> functions used in Rathjen's original OCF are also not so easy to understand, and differ from the <math>\chi</math> functions defined above.

Rathjen's <math>\psi</math> and the simplification provided above are not the same OCF. This is partially because the former is known to admit an ordinal notation, while the latter isn't known to admit an ordinal notation.{{Citation needed|date=October 2022}} Rathjen's <math>\psi</math> is often confounded with another of his OCFs which also uses the symbol <math>\psi</math>, but they are distinct notions. The former one is a published OCF, while the latter one is just a function symbol in an ordinal notation associated to an unpublished OCF.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rathjen|first=Michael|date=1989-09-04|title=Proof-theoretic analysis of KPM|url=http://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/KPM-Ordinal-Analysis.pdf|access-date=2021-09-18|website=University of Leeds}}</ref>
